title: The Impact Ladder
author: Clark, Jamie Lee
summary: This edition of DistillED lays out Thomas Guskey's five-level model for evaluating professional development and argues that most school CPD evaluation stops at the least meaningful level. Clark's central claim is that PD must be 'planned backward': leaders should first specify the desired student outcome, then work down through the classroom practice, organizational support, and teacher learning that would have to precede it, and only then design the training session itself. She contrasts this with the common practice of running a training and only ever collecting 'happy sheet' reaction data, which Guskey himself calls the easiest but least informative measure of impact. Drawing on Sims et al.'s meta-analysis, she adds a diagnostic layer — insight, goals, technique, and practice — for figuring out exactly where an otherwise sound PD program fails to reach the classroom. The piece closes with a five-step practical protocol that turns Guskey's academic ladder into something a department can actually run, ending on the claim that PD only 'worked' if practice changed, survived an ordinary week, and the named outcome moved.
points: CPD should be planned backward from the desired student outcome, not forward from whatever course or speaker was booked.
End-of-session 'happy sheets' measure whether people enjoyed the training, not whether anything changed — file that as logistics feedback, not impact evidence.
When a walk-through shows no change in practice, diagnose which of four ingredients is missing — insight, goals, technique, or practice — rather than concluding 'the training didn't work.'
Real evidence of impact requires two checks spaced weeks apart: one to see if a technique got used at all, a later one to see if it survived an ordinary week.
A technique that held up in classrooms but didn't move the target outcome is still useful diagnostic information, not proof nothing was learned.
quotes: In planning professional development to improve student learning, the order of these levels must be reversed. You must plan "backward." — Thomas R. Guskey, Does It Make a Difference? Evaluating Professional Development, Educational Leadership (2002)
end-of-session feedback is 'the most common form of professional development evaluations, and the easiest type of information to gather and analyze.'

Some educators, he notes, call these measures 'happiness quotients': they tell us how participants reacted to the experience, not whether they learned anything, changed their practice, or improved student outcomes.
Teachers might understand the idea but not know how to use it, or learn the technique but lack the support to keep using it. A Rung 1 feedback form won't tell you that.
You do not need to turn school PD into a research project. You need to stop treating the easiest evidence as the most important evidence.
Your PD worked if all three hold: classroom practice changed, that change survived an ordinary week, and the outcome you named at the start moved.
